item.title: This Is Not the Child I Dreamed of Having
item.description:
Parenting

This Is Not the Child I Dreamed of Having

Approaching a child's gender transition with mindfulness can ease the process.

Posted July 11, 2026

Key points
  • Many parents have trouble when a child decides to transition to a different gender.
  • Children often do not get the support they need from family and community.
  • Mindfulness can help both parents and children accept change.
  • The entire family can benefit from compassion.

“What the hell are you doing?” my patient Dan screamed at his 4-year-old son, who was dressed in his wife’s floral apron and twirling a whisk.

“I’m cooking, Daddy,” Bobby responded as he started to cry.

“I felt like such a jerk,” Dan told me. “I know I’m not the poster child for gentle parenting, and I know I shouldn’t have yelled, but I can’t stand it when he wears his sister’s pink dresses and plays with her dolls. I dreamed of having a child who played football, the way I did, and my father did.” He paused. “He’ll grow out of this, won’t he?” Dan asked in a voice that was almost pleading.

For the past 30 years, I’ve worked with parents who have struggled with the gender choices that their children are making. Sometimes they berate themselves, other times they take out their rage on their children. Often, family members compound the guilt and shame. Years ago, it was often unusual for children to want to transition in middle school or high school, but we are now seeing this conversation arise as early as elementary school.

I’ve seen this anguish from many perspectives. I trained at a college counseling center in the mid-1980s when gender questioning was uncharted territory, and there was little support for teenagers to come to terms with the complexities of sexual desire that challenged the traditional norms. And the issue of sexuality emerges full force in college when students are away from home and family.

But change is not easy for anyone. Eileen, a very polished executive, entered my office and began to sob. She had never lost her composure in our three years of therapy, which focused on her early trauma. “I feel torn between my head and heart, and there is no one to talk to about this.” She explained that Sara, now 14, wanted to be male, and was asking their classmates and teachers to use the name “Sam.” The teachers and other kids were accommodating. However, in Scouts, there was teasing and bullying from other girls. Sara developed an eating disorder. It was hard to get support from family. The grandfather, from a very different generation, could not understand what was happening. “I miss my sweet little girl,” he lamented, causing everyone to cringe. Sara ran to the bathroom to cry and wouldn’t speak to him for months.

"I know I’m not supposed to say this, but I had dreams of doing conventional girly things with Sara, like clothes shopping, or going to rom-com movies. Nope. That is not going to happen."

After watching the heartache of parents for decades, I have come up with suggestions that have been helpful for many.

Don’t Do This Alone.

Many parents feel that they have lost a child in this process. They are aware that this isn’t the death of their child, but the child they are now parenting is not who they imagined. Finding others who are struggling in the same way can be comforting, whether it's an online group or chat, or locating support at the local hospital, church, or other place of worship. It is OK to allow yourself to grieve. Give yourself the space to have ambivalent feelings.

Learn to Love the Child Who Is Present.

Mindfulness has been a major support for the parents (and children) I work with, as change is one of the basic maxims of mindfulness. Can you bring compassion for everyone in the family? Change is a constant, in everything. Watching your child change is part of nature. This change was not anticipated, but then nothing is. And we can’t control our lives, or the lives of our children. This perspective added some comfort as Sara transitioned to Sam, complete with surgery and hormones.

What was especially helpful for Eileen was that Sam didn’t seem so “tortured” as she put it. They are finding increased comfort in being in their body. “Mom,” Sam commented, “this is who I am supposed to be. I like who I am.”

They had always been interested in music, studying piano, singing, and guitar when young. But now, as Sam, they could find a new sound.

“I’m finding I like this new voice,” Eileen commented. The lyrics are edgy, the beat is strong, and the music is fresh and new. Sam and his band have developed a following, and a recording label is talking about a deal. It has been a huge change for all of us, but we have worked together to find our way. It is not what I wanted, but I find that we all have become more resilient.

item.title: When Healthy Eating Becomes Unhealthy
item.description:
Eating Disorders

When Healthy Eating Becomes Unhealthy

Exploring the psychological costs of nutritionism.

Posted July 11, 2026

Key points
  • Nutritionism reduces food to nutrients, overlooking the broader context of health.
  • Social media and wellness marketing often fuel anxiety by promoting nutritional optimization.
  • Rigid food rules can contribute to anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and eating disorders.
  • Psychological flexibility around food is an important part of overall health.

Most of us have heard the message that food is medicine. Research has consistently shown that eating patterns can influence health. But somewhere along the way, many of us stopped seeing food as something that nourishes, satisfies, connects us with others, and brings pleasure. Instead, food has increasingly become a collection of protein grams, fiber targets, antioxidants, and micronutrients to optimize. This way of thinking has a name: nutritionism.

Coined by Australian sociologist Gyorgy Scrinis and later popularized by journalist Michael Pollan, nutritionism describes the tendency to reduce food to its individual nutrients while overlooking the complexity of how people actually eat and live. Health becomes something we believe we can achieve by optimizing nutrients rather than considering the whole picture. While nutrition science can absolutely inform our understanding of health, nutritionism often strips that science of context.

The Illusion of Control

Source: Jan Sedivy/Unsplash

Health is determined by much more than what appears on our plates. Sleep, stress, genetics, relationships, movement, financial resources, access to healthcare, and emotional health all influence how we feel and function. Yet nutrition marketing often suggests that if we simply eat the right foods, avoid the wrong ingredients, and optimize every meal, we can control our health and eliminate uncertainty.

That message is appealing because certainty feels reassuring. The wellness industry often capitalizes on that anxiety. There is always another nutrient to optimize, another ingredient to fear, another supplement to buy, or another eating strategy promising better health.

Social media only amplifies these messages. Nutrition myths frequently oversimplify complex biological processes or present rigid habits as universal truths. Algorithms reward certainty, not nuance. "Never eat after 7 p.m." or "This food causes inflammation" spreads much faster than "The answer depends."

When Healthy Eating Starts Hurting Mental Health

As a psychotherapist specializing in eating disorders, I rarely see people whose struggles begin with a desire to become unhealthy. More often than not, they begin by wanting to eat "better." Over time, those intentions can become increasingly rigid. Meals are carefully calculated. Food labels are scrutinized. Entire food groups are eliminated. Eating out becomes stressful. Social events are avoided because the food feels unpredictable. Thoughts about eating can consume hours of the day.

For some people, these patterns become intertwined with anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), or eating disorders. The problem is not nutrition knowledge itself. The problem is when nutrition becomes a source of fear, self-worth, or perceived control.

Context Matters More Than the Food

The same nutrition recommendation can have very different effects depending on the person receiving it. A recommendation that is neutral or even helpful for one person may reinforce fear, rigidity, or compulsive behaviors in someone struggling with an eating disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), or health anxiety. The context in which it is given matters. For example, someone might choose to eat a simple rather than a complex carbohydrate before a workout because it is digested more quickly and provides readily available energy. On its own, that is simply a nutrition choice.

The picture changes when food choices are driven primarily by fear. If someone is terrified of weight gain, rigidly follows food rules, eliminates entire food groups, carefully tracks macronutrients and micronutrients, or feels compelled to optimize every eating decision, the nutritional rationale may be serving a psychological function rather than a nutritional one. Nutrition science can become a way to justify restriction, reduce anxiety, reinforce compulsive behaviors, or create a sense of certainty and control.

There is a particular irony here. Someone may become intensely focused on optimizing nutrition to build muscle, improve athletic performance, or maximize health while simultaneously becoming so fearful of weight gain that eating becomes increasingly rigid and consuming. Hunger and satisfaction are ignored in favor of numbers. Meals are judged by whether they are "optimal" rather than whether they are nourishing or satisfying. Food becomes something to manage rather than something to enjoy. At that point, the pursuit of "optimal" nutrition has moved far away from health.

Health Includes Psychological Flexibility

Ironically, the relentless pursuit of perfect nutrition can undermine both mental and physical health. Chronic anxiety around food, social isolation, rigid restriction, and constant self-monitoring all carry consequences of their own. For most people, good health does not require micromanaging every macro- and micronutrient or eating with mathematical precision. Consistently following a varied and flexible pattern of eating is supported by far more evidence than striving for nutritional perfection.

As a therapist, I often remind people that a healthy relationship with food includes flexibility. It leaves room for enjoyment, culture, connection, and trust in our bodies. Health isn't defined by how perfectly we eat. It's reflected in whether food supports our lives rather than consumes them.
